analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 10% through 2030.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 6, 2025 by one Democrat and one Republican, the bill sits in the House Financial Services Committee with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent, including all finance charges, and block issuers from using fees to get around the cap. A cardholder who is charged more could sue to recover every dollar of interest, finance charges, or fees paid within two years, and a knowingly violating lender forfeits all interest on the debt. Existing consumer agencies could also enforce it, and state laws offering stronger protection stay intact. The cap would end on January 1, 2031 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry a credit card balance from month to month. Most revolving card rates run well above 20 percent, so a 10 percent cap plus a fee shield and a private right of action would directly cut the cost of carrying debt and give borrowers a way to claw back overcharges in court [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 10 percent, inclusive of all finance charges [S3].
Bars lenders from using fees that are not counted as finance charges to evade the cap, and limits the total of such fees to the total finance charges [S3].
Lets a borrower sue within two years to recover the entire amount of interest, finance charges, or fees paid above the cap, and makes a knowing violator forfeit all interest on the debt [S2][S3].
Adds the cap to the Truth in Lending Act's civil penalty provisions, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission, and preserves stronger state laws [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — major banks and other lenders — would lose a large share of the interest and fee revenue they now collect from borrowers who revolve balances. Some issuers would respond by tightening credit standards or limiting rewards, which would fall hardest on borrowers with weaker credit.

drawbacks.text: A hard price cap can shrink access to credit: issuers facing a 10 percent ceiling may raise approval standards, cut credit lines, or steer away from customers whose risk would not be profitable to serve at that rate [S3].
The bill limits total non-finance-charge fees but does not ban them, so issuers could restructure revenue into permitted fees up to the amount of finance charges [S3].
The cap expires on January 1, 2031, so the relief is temporary unless Congress extends it [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of households that carry credit card debt, the benefit is direct and large: lower rates, a shield against fee workarounds, and a court remedy for overcharges. The main cost is that some riskier borrowers could lose access to card credit as issuers reprice risk, and the sunset means the protection must be renewed. On balance the bill delivers a substantial, concrete benefit to ordinary borrowers at a cost concentrated on a highly profitable industry, though the temporary sunset and the fee limit being partial keep it from being airtight.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 6, 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on March 6, 2025, joined by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, and the action history shows no further steps since [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers keep collecting today's rates, which often exceed 20 percent, while the bill waits in committee. Borrowers carrying balances are no worse off than before but have gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the 10 Percent Credit Card Interest Rate Cap Act on March 6, 2025

for.name: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna
for.role: Sole cosponsor, U.S. House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a two-party sponsorship

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — but the bill has attracted no cosponsors beyond its two original members and no committee action.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (major banks and consumer lenders)
industries.note: The bill caps card APRs at 10 percent, below the roughly 20-plus percent rates commonly charged on revolving balances, and forfeits all interest for knowing violators — a direct hit to one of banking's most profitable lines of business. The industry has no financial stake in the bill's passage and its gain runs against borrowers' savings [S3].

industries.industry: Debt collectors and creditors facing repayment actions
industries.note: Borrowers could sue within two years to recover all interest, finance charges, and fees paid above the cap, creating new repayment liability for lenders [S3].

analysis.trajectory: With only two sponsors, no cosponsors added since introduction, and no action in the Financial Services Committee five months in, the bill's realistic path is to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless a committee chair schedules a hearing or it gets attached to larger financial legislation, which the current level of support makes unlikely.
